summary: This memo describes how to carry DTMF signals, other tones and telephony events in RTP packets. It replaces RFC 2833, keeping only basic event codes and creating an IANA registry for more. It makes DTMF support optional, with implementations indicating supported events, and adds segmenting, multiple events per packet and state events.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4733 defines ways to carry telephone signals in Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) packets. A packet can name an event, such as a keypad digit, or describe a tone by its sound properties.

questions: how are dtmf digits sent over rtp
subtitle: Two RTP payload formats carry named phone events or describe the tones themselves.

tldr.problem: Speech codecs may distort tones that machines need to recognize, and some telephone signals are events rather than sounds.
tldr.mechanism: The telephone-event format identifies an event and reports its growing duration. The tone format describes frequencies, modulation, volume, and duration.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4733 replaces RFC 2833, makes supported events subject to negotiation, and adds procedures for long events, combined events, and state events. It is updated by RFC 4734 and RFC 5244.

today: RFC 4733 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2833 and is updated by RFC 4734 and RFC 5244. It has not itself been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Telephone Signals Need a Format
sections.content:
RFC 4733 defines two RTP payload formats. telephone-event carries DTMF digits and other named telephone events. tone describes tones using their frequencies and cadence.

Separate formats help because low-rate speech codecs may not reproduce tones accurately enough for automatic recognition. Named events can also carry out-of-band signals, such as on-hook, that cannot be represented as tones. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2833.
sections.plainLanguage: Speech audio can change a tone enough to make it hard for a machine to identify. RTP can instead carry an event name or a description of the tone.

sections.title: The Telephone-Event Payload
sections.content:
The telephone-event payload has an event code, an end bit, a reserved bit, a volume value, and a duration. The event code is between 0 and 255. The timestamp marks the start of the event, and packets updating the same event retain that timestamp while reporting a larger cumulative duration.

The default clock rate is 8000 Hz. A duration of zero is reserved for events defined as states. Events are negotiated out of band; a sender must restrict itself to events the receiver lists, and if no list arrives it should assume only DTMF events 0 through 15.
sections.plainLanguage: A telephone-event packet identifies a signal and reports how long it has lasted. Repeated packets update the same event, so the receiver can track its duration.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Events
sections.content:
A sender should begin reporting an event as soon as it recognizes it. Updates use the same timestamp and increasing cumulative duration; an update interval of 50 ms is recommended. The first packet marks the event's start, and the final packet marks its end.

The sender should transmit the final report three times in total so the receiver can recover the end if a packet is lost. If an event exceeds the largest duration value, the sender splits it into contiguous segments. Multiple events may share a packet only when they are consecutive and have no overlap or pause.

Receivers use timestamps and durations to decide when to play events, not the spacing between packets. Their playout method balances packet loss against the risk of extending a tone too long.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender reports an event while it continues, then repeats the final report to improve the chance that the receiver gets it. Long events can be divided into consecutive segments.

sections.title: The DTMF Event Codes
sections.content:
This RFC initially defines sixteen named events for DTMF. Digits 0 through 9 use their digit values, the star key uses code 10, the pound key uses code 11, and A through D use codes 12 through 15.

The RFC no longer requires every implementation to support every DTMF event. Implementations describe the events they can handle, and senders use that information when choosing which events to transmit. Other event codes can be registered if their meaning and application are documented and existing codes are not sufficient.
sections.plainLanguage: Each DTMF key has a numeric event code. Sender and receiver agree on the supported codes before those events are sent.

sections.title: Describing a Tone by Its Sound
sections.content:
The tone payload describes a sound instead of naming the event. Its first word gives modulation frequency, a divide-by-three flag, volume, and duration. Following words give one or more frequencies to combine; a frequency of zero means silence.

Each tone packet stands on its own. Unlike telephone-event packets, successive tone packets use advancing timestamps, with each new timestamp equal to the preceding timestamp plus its duration. A lost packet therefore leaves a gap in the information, and the RFC recommends redundant reporting when greater reliability is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The tone format tells the receiver which frequencies to combine, how loud they are, and how long to play them. Each packet describes its own time interval.

sections.title: Packet Loss and Congestion
sections.content:
The RFC identifies lost events, late starts, incorrect durations, gaps in playback, and excessive delay as performance problems. A receiver can add playout delay to absorb network variation, but this increases end-to-end delay.

Telephone-event updates carry the event history so a receiver can recover from some lost packets. Repeating the final report helps communicate the end. During congestion, a sender may increase the packetization interval to reduce packet frequency, but the receiver then needs more delay.
sections.plainLanguage: Repeated event updates help a receiver handle packet loss, while a playback buffer can reduce gaps. Longer waits improve recovery but add delay.

sections.title: Integrity and Confidentiality
sections.content:
The payload formats inherit the security considerations of RTP and the RTP profile in use. A one-bit change in a compressed telephone-event payload can greatly change its meaning, so message integrity must be provided for that payload.

Implementations should support Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) for confidentiality and integrity. The RFC notes that the appropriate key-distribution method depends on the application.
sections.plainLanguage: A small change to an event packet can alter the signal it represents. The packet therefore needs integrity protection, and SRTP can also protect its contents.

viz.caption: FIELDS IN A NAMED TELEPHONE EVENT

fields.name: E
fields.desc: Marks the end of the event.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; senders set it to zero.

fields.name: Volume
fields.desc: Tone power level when volume applies.

fields.name: Duration
fields.desc: Elapsed event duration in timestamp units.
